title: From First Commits to Graduation: Reflecting on 8 Months at Road to Wiki Cohort 2!
content:
Celebrating growth, community, open-source impact, and high-octane memories in Gurugram!

Dates: 2 and 3 October 2026
Event: Graduation Day for Road to Wiki Cohort 2

Eight months ago, an ambitious group of developers set off on a journey into the world of open source. Organized by WikiClub Tech India and Open Knowledge India (OKI) at IIIT Hyderabad, out of over 200+ applicants who filled out the form, 50 developers embarked on this journey to become core open-source contributors.

Stepping into the role of Dev-Circle Lead meant working directly with student developers facing real-world engineering challenges. Navigating large-scale open-source ecosystems can feel daunting initially, so our focus was turning confusion into momentum.

  • Tackling Setup Blockers: We spent late nights working through environment issues, matching Node.js versions, configuring SSH keys, learning Gerrit code review rules, and setting up git commit hooks.
  • First Merges Across Wikimedia: Watching mentees land their first code merge was a high point of the program. Together, we contributed across several major projects, including MediaWiki core, MinervaNeue, GrowthExperiments, ProofreadPage, and Wikispeech.
snippet:
Celebrating growth, community, open-source impact, and high-octane memories in Gurugram!

title: Wikimedia Foundation Bulletin 2026 Issue 19
content:
Here is a quick overview of highlights from the Wikimedia Foundation since our last issue on September 25. Previous editions of this bulletin are on Meta. Let foundationbulletin@wikimedia.org know if you have any feedback or suggestions for improvement!

  • Community Wishlist: Community Wishlist is looking for volunteers to join their working group. You can find details on the goal of the group, roles and expectations, norms we’ll follow, and how to sign up on this Meta-Wiki page.
  • Human knowledge at stake: Wikimedia Foundation makes the case for human knowledge at the UN General Assembly and how scrapers are straining our infrastructure and the larger human knowledge ecosystem online.
  • Joy of contributing: How a simple thanks fuelled one of our Wikimedians of the Year as they connect the community.
  • PTAC technical topics: The Product and Technology Advisory Council calls for the community to suggest topics that it should consider and discuss with the Wikimedia Foundation. Submit your topic on the council’s talk page.

title: Bringing Wiki Projects to the 2026 Summer Institute in Computational Social Science in Kenya
content:
Wait, you can just access all that knowledge and even contribute to it?!

A SICSS participant when learning about Wikimedia projects

Wait, you can just access all that knowledge and even contribute to it?!

A SICSS participant when learning about Wikimedia projects

It takes a village of people with different skills to create, maintain and learn from open knowledge. And the 2026 edition of the Kenyan Summer Institute in Computational Social Science (SICSS) offered just the place for that, by bringing together social scientists, technologists, and Wikimedians to learn from each other.

Since 2017, the SICSS events bring together scholars in computational social science in different locations around the world for two intense weeks of project-based learning, in which early career researchers are trained in computational methods during the first week. Those newly learned skills are then directly applied to concrete, co-designed group research projects during the second week. And in many cases continue onwards beyond the project window.

title: Strengthening Language Communities in the Open Movement: Reflections from the Inaugural Language Diversity Conference
content:
From 2 to 4 October 2026, Accra, Ghana, became a gathering point for people working to preserve, document, strengthen, and advance the world’s linguistic diversity.

The inaugural Language Diversity Conference was held at Fiesta Royale Hotel under the theme “Strengthening Language Communities in the Open Movement.”

The conference was organized by the Dagbani Wikimedians User Group, in collaboration with Wikitongues, Wikimedia UK, and Language Diversity Hub, with funding from the Wikimedia Foundation.

Welcoming the global language community to Accra. Participants began arriving on 1 October from different parts of the world. As members of the local organizing team, we were responsible for welcoming participants and managing registration.

title: Tech News 2026 – Issue 42
content:
Latest tech news from the Wikimedia technical community. Please tell other users about these changes. Not all changes will affect you. Translations are available.

Weekly highlight

  • Starting October 13, wikis can change the default pattern for auto-generated reference names in VisualEditor (currently <ref name=":1" />). They will be able to use human-readable, content-based reference names that are more helpful to contributors using the source editor (e.g. <ref name="Miller2026-1" />). VisualEditor reference name patterns can be defined using MediaWiki system messages, JSON, templates and modules (more information). Admins can enable these changes via community configuration. This is a community wish implemented by WMDE Technical Wishes. [1]
  • Sub-referencing is a new MediaWiki feature that allows editors to reuse references with different details. It will be deployed to English Wikipedia on October 14 and to remaining Wikimedia Foundation wikis by end of October (likely October 21). The FAQ lists possible actions to take on your wiki to support the deployment. This is a long-standing community wish implemented by WMDE Technical Wishes. [2][3]

title: An AI bot for polishing Malayalam Wikipedia articles
content:
In a Malayalam Wikipedia article about cricket, Everton Weekes was not a man. He was ആഴ്ചകൾ (aazhchakal), the Malayalam word for “weeks”. His surname was machine-translated. In a physics article, a textbook was credited to an author named പുൽത്തകിടി (pulthakidi), “lawn”; the author’s surname was Lawn.

Errors like these sat on their pages for years, unnoticed, because the Malayalam reads perfectly like Malayalam. Thousands of our articles were translated from other languages, and many are still waiting for a second pass. Our community simply has too few editors to clean up the kind of mess that translation sometimes leaves behind. That is what led me to look for a solution involving AI, and to build a bot called AksharaBot, named from the Malayalam word അക്ഷരം (aksharam), meaning “letter”.

In August 2026, I proposed this AI-powered bot for Malayalam Wikipedia. To be fully transparent about how it works, I put its most awkward quality at the center of the request for the community to judge:

title: The Story of WikiTour: How It Started, What We Learned, and Where We Hope to Go
content:
From our point of view, as Kent Wiki Club alumni (Jjurieee and Blusjai)

Every language carries stories. It carries the names of places, the wisdom of elders, the stories passed from one generation to another, and the ways communities understand the world around them. Yet, when we look at the digital world, many of these languages remain largely invisible.

For us, WikiTour began with a simple question:

What if our students could become the people who put their own languages on the map of the internet?

The journey began in 2024, when Kent Wikimedia Club, Kent Campus Institute of Teacher Education, Tuaran, Sabah together with Wikimedia Community User Group Malaysia (WCUGM), held the first WikiTour at three locations: Universiti Pendidikan Sultan Idris (UPSI), Sarawak State Education Department, and Sandakan National Secondary School.

title: Meet MEOW: An Easier Way to Discover Wikimedia Learning Resources
content:
Across the Wikimedia movement, people are creating presentations, publishing reports, organising workshops, and sharing lessons from their projects. These resources can help others develop new skills and build partnerships, but finding them is not always easy, because of the nature of the internet, they are spread across different platforms and languages, and useful experiences can be difficult to discover.

For this, MEOW (Metabase Educational Open Works, https://meow.toolforge.org/), offers an easier way to explore this shared knowledge. Whether you are preparing a workshop, planning a partnership, or learning about a new topic, it helps you find resources from across the movement.

MEOW is a free interface for browsing the resources cataloged in Metabase. It is easy to use and you do not need an account or any knowledge of query languages to use it.
snippet: Across the Wikimedia movement, people are creating presentations, publishing reports, organising workshops, and sharing lessons from their projects. These resources can help others develop new skills
creator: Alicia Fagerving (WMSE)

title: From Madagascar to Accra: Reflections from the Language Diversity Conference 2026
content:
Participating in the Language Diversity Conference 2026 in Accra, Ghana, was a meaningful experience for me, both personally and as someone working to strengthen the presence of the Malagasy language in the digital world.

The conference brought together more than 100 language activists, Wikimedians, researchers, and heritage workers representing 82 languages. For three days, Accra became a space for sharing experiences, learning from different communities, and discussing how languages can remain visible and active in an increasingly digital world.

The conference opened with Jara dance, Nbangba Cultural Troupe from Ghana, immediately bringing a strong sense of culture, identity, and community into the event. It was a beautiful way to begin a conference about languages. Before the keynote, presentations, and discussions even started, we were already seeing that language is closely connected to culture, traditions, identity, and the way communities express themselves.

That cultural atmosphere remained present throughout the conference.

I was particularly happy to see the Malagasy language represented at an international conference dedicated to language diversity.
snippet: Participating in the Language Diversity Conference 2026 in Accra, Ghana, was a meaningful experience for me, both personally and as someone working to strengthen the presence of the Malagasy language
creator: Mammysou17

title: Inaugural Wikimedia Kimaragang Online Meetup: Strengthening Community, Empowering Digital Knowledge
content:
Following the previous physical meetup, the Wikimedia Kimaragang Community successfully organized its Online Meetup Series 1 on September 19, 2026, from 8:00 PM to 9:00 PM. This first online gathering for the community was conducted under the guidance of the Wikimedia Community User Group Malaysia (WCUGM). The session, moderated by the meetup coordinator (Blusjai), was attended by 10 Kimaragang community members, 2 WCUGM representatives (Tofeiku, Rulwarih), and 1 representative from the Kadazandusun Language community (Jjurieee).

The session began with an introduction to the Wikimedia Foundation and WCUGM. During this briefing, emphasis was placed on Wikimedia’s core mission: making knowledge freely accessible to all. This mission was directly linked to the potential of the Kimaragang ethnic group to enhance global access to information regarding their culture and language. Additionally, Wikimedia platforms were highlighted as a space for the community to interact and exchange ideas without geographical boundaries.

title: Wiki for Human Rights Nigeria: First Language Wikipedia Physical Training
content:
In August, Wiki for Human Rights Nigeria launched its first-language Wikipedia physical training. Since the start of the project catering to LGBTIQ+ people, the organization has mostly focused on training queer people to edit Wikipedia, add structured data on Wikidata, upload images to Wikimedia Commons, and become acquainted with what Wikimedia projects entail. Still, we never explored what it means to contribute to the local-language Wikimedia projects.

Much of the early work on queer topics on Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba Wikipedia came through our writing contests. Those contributions matter, but our goal now is to grow a community of editors who stay with this work beyond a contest, as allies invested in advancing queer rights in Nigeria. This organizing has also come at a cost: I have received hostile messages from people opposed to our work, which is part of why building a committed, supportive community matters so much.

title: Leaves from The Story of My Journey to Kaohsiung
content:
I had the opportunity to attend the ESEAP Conference in May 2026 as a scholar. It was my first in-person meeting with colleagues and friends from the ESEAP Wikimedia Hub, and my second overseas experience with the global Wikimedia movement after the 2025 GLAM Wiki Conference in Lisbon. I arrived with one question: how can our communities grow technical contributions, from MediaWiki and templates to Wikidata reuse?

I landed on Thursday, 14 May, and promptly spent 45 minutes in immigration, the first time I had ever been detained. My papers were complete, including my E-TAC (Taiwan’s online arrival permit, which I used on the strength of my past Schengen visa). The real problem was the faded Portuguese entry and exit stamps, which the officers could not read until someone brought out a magnifying glass. Lesson learned: ask officers to press firmly when stamping. At the time I was sure I would be deported. Now I smile while remembering it.

Then I stepped outside, and the Kaohsiung sun and wind hit my face. It was stinging hot, exactly like Jakarta or Surabaya at midday. Pulling my suitcase, I smiled. It felt like home.

title: Three Days of Learning, Collaboration and Editing for Electoral Integrity
content:
From 28 to 30 September 2026, I participated in the Interactive Media Seminar for Electoral Integrity in Abuja, Nigeria. Organised by FIAP through FactCheckAfrica, in collaboration with Wikimedia User Group Nigeria, the seminar brought together Wikimedia editors, journalists, newsroom editors and fact-checkers to explore how reliable information can be documented and made accessible ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections.

For me, the three days were an opportunity to learn, exchange ideas and put Wikimedia’s editorial principles into practice. I came away with a better understanding of how the work of journalists, fact-checkers and Wikimedia contributors can complement one another in addressing misinformation and disinformation.

The first day focused on Wikipedia’s approach to reliable information and the principles that guide its content. We discussed verifiability, reliable sourcing, neutral point of view and the prohibition against original research. We also explored how transparency and community participation help maintain the quality of Wikipedia articles.
